source.title: Crafting a Good Prompt or Providing Exemplary Dialogues? A Study of In-Context Learning for Persona-based Dialogue Generation
source.authors: Jiashu Pu; Ya-Jing Wan; Yuru Zhang; Jing Chen; Ling Cheng; Qian Shao; Yongzhu Chang; Tang-Jie Lv; Rong-Sheng Zhang

page_placements.theme: ICL that copying can't explain runs through FFNs, other subspaces or non-induction heads

record.tranche_reason: The authors use their own dialogue-generation experiments to argue that n-gram/induction-head explanations cannot fully account for the ICL effects they observe. They do not directly measure induction heads or the versions’ specified token-copying or training-loss behaviours.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses induction heads as an incomplete explanation, but does not identify, intervene on, or measure induction heads, token-position loss, or their formation during training. Its dialogue response-quality results are relevant to the topic but do not measure the behaviours specified by V1–V7; they are recorded as none. The paper also cites prior work on induction heads, which is not treated as a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study measures persona-dialogue response quality from GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Ernie under corrupted demonstrations. It never identifies, ablates or measures induction heads, and never measures loss by token index or training dynamics. Its claim that induction or n-gram heads 'cannot fully account' for the results (§8, §A.6.1) is a verbal argument. That argument rests on a different construct (evaluator-scored response quality). It therefore discusses V3/V6 rather than testing them. T6 rather than the reader's T5, since no result bears on any version's measure.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors add that prompt tuning is the most cost-effective lever, and that random demo retrieval beats similarity or same-context retrieval. They state explicitly that they do not investigate ICL's underlying mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates prompt and demonstration settings for persona-based Chinese dialogue generation; it does not reproduce the original induction-head identification or training-trajectory method.
record.method_sensitivity: Dialogue response-quality outcomes vary by model and demo corruption type. The paper also varies demo retrieval, context length, and few-shot count; the stated trends are not equally evident across models.

fits_no_version.finding: With k=5, response quality with demos whose turns and tokens are both shuffled stays above Context Only. GPT-3.5: 0.160−0.000 vs 0.147. GPT-4: 0.235−0.062 vs 0.155. Ernie: 0.487−0.042 vs 0.345. Token shuffling within turns lowers quality significantly for GPT-4 and Ernie.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLMs gain in persona-dialogue ICL from demonstrations whose sequential order is destroyed. This is presented by the authors as hard to explain by induction/n-gram copying alone.

fits_no_version.finding: Response quality under fully corrupted demos trends upward with k. The authors say this is not evident for GPT-4. Values are figure-only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More corrupted demonstrations can still improve dialogue ICL quality, model-dependently.

record.problems: The paper reports experiments on a compact evaluation set with 6 personas and three selected LLMs; it does not directly measure induction heads or the loss-by-token behaviour at issue. Many scaling results are presented only in figures, and detailed values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the paper’s other prompt/retrieval comparisons, since they do not bear on the induction-head claims. The additional figure-only rows retain the directly relevant corrupted-demo scaling trend; other figure series are not catalogued.

untested.parts: No head identification, previous-token composition, or [A][B]…[A]→[B] test.
No training trajectory, formation timing, or loss-curve bump.
No induction-head measurement or ablation; no loss by token index. Response quality under shuffled demos is not that measure.
No induction-head detection in any model.
No training or data manipulation affecting head formation.
Corrupted-demo response quality is reported, but no heads or mechanisms are identified as carriers. The anti-induction argument is verbal only.

record.verdict_notes: The induction-head argument (§A.6.1) assumes shuffled n-grams leave nothing for induction heads to use. Yet shuffled demos still carry the token distribution, which copying could exploit; Fig. 2 shows a substantial share of output tokens drawn from demos. So the argument does not rule out induction heads. The evaluator is a self-trained RoBERTa with Spearman 0.378 against expert ratings. The test set has only 6 personas.

versions.untested_parts: No head identification, previous-token-head composition, or [A][B] … [A] → [B] copying test.
No training trajectory, induction-head formation timing, in-context-learning loss-by-token measure, or loss-curve bump.
No induction-head intervention or measurement of most in-context learning as token-index loss reduction; dialogue response quality is not that measure.
No cross-family, size, run, architecture, or modality test for induction-behaviour heads.
The paper varies demo properties for dialogue ICL, but does not test their effect on induction-head formation or the specified token-index ICL behaviour.
The paper varies demo labels and content but does not test few-shot task learning against induction heads or identify other heads/mechanisms as its main carrier.
No analysis of induction-head formation sub-steps or overlapping training transitions.

relation.reason: Section A.6.1 discusses induction-head explanations and argues they cannot fully explain improvements from corrupted demonstrations, without testing any listed claim version.

tranche.reason: Dialogue response quality under demonstration corruption measures a different construct from the claim versions. The study does not identify induction heads, establish their causal contribution, or measure token-index loss or training transitions.

source_check.notes: The statement's numbers match Table 1, but its cited rows do not cover the GPT-4 and Ernie double-shuffle results. The authors explicitly leave underlying ICL mechanisms uninvestigated.
